title: Bharata's journey
hook: a prince wakes from a bad dream, and riders arrive who won't tell him why they've come

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's death and the curse, part three. The king died past midnight, the body was kept in oil, and riders left for Kekaya with orders to say nothing. Did you reach out to someone older? Day five hundred forty-five.

Far to the northwest, in his grandfather's city, Bharata wakes up badly shaken. His friends try to cheer him with music and jokes, and he can't smile. He tells them about the dream. His father, pale, hair loose, smeared with oil, riding a chariot pulled by donkeys, heading south. In the old Indian imagination, south is the direction of the dead. Bharata says: either I, or Rama, or Lakshmana, or the king is going to die. And that same day, the riders from Ayodhya arrive.
screen: `A DREAM IN KEKAYA.` → `A CHARIOT HEADING SOUTH.` → `THE RIDERS ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: The messengers do exactly as they were told. Your family's priest sends his greetings, they say. There's urgent business. Come at once. Bharata asks after everyone, one by one: his father, Rama, Lakshmana, the three queens. And the messengers give him careful, polite answers that are not quite answers. All is well, they say, with those you ask about. So he takes leave of his grandfather and sets out, and the journey home takes days. Valmiki gives us the road, the rivers crossed, the towns passed. And then Ayodhya appears, and something is wrong. No music. No crowds. The gardens look neglected, the streets are quiet, the people avoid his eyes. Bharata says to the charioteer: this isn't my city. He goes straight to his father's rooms, and his father isn't there. So he goes to his mother. Kaikeyi is glad to see him. She asks about the journey, about her family. And then she tells him, almost lightly: your father has gone the way all living things go. Bharata falls to the floor. When he can speak, he asks, where is Rama? I want to touch his feet. He's my father now. And Kaikeyi, believing she's giving him good news, tells him the rest: the two boons, the exile, the throne kept for him. She thinks she has made her son a king. She has no idea what she's about to hear back.
screen: `ALL IS WELL, THE RIDERS SAY.` · `A CITY GONE QUIET.` · `YOUR FATHER HAS GONE THE WAY OF ALL.` · `WHERE IS RAMA? HE'S MY FATHER NOW.` · then, large: `SHE THINKS IT'S GOOD NEWS.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Imagine coming home after a long trip, to a street you know well. Walk it slowly in your mind: the turn, the doorway, the sound of your own key. Notice what you'd expect to see, and how quickly you'd sense if something were off. Then let the picture go, and just feel where you're sitting now, the floor, the air, the breath. This place, right now, is enough to come home to. The bell holds the time.
Bharata's journey. Called home from Kekaya without being told why, Bharata finds a silent city, and learns from his mother that his father is dead and his brother exiled.
Your line: Bharata's journey. Today, when you walk into a room, notice the mood before you speak. Day five hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Many Ramayana tellers treat Bharata's return as the start of a new story inside the old one, and his first question for Rama, not for the throne, is often quoted in sermons and recitations.

fork.setup: you're Bharata. your mother has just told you your father is dead. what do you ask first?
fork.reveal: he asks for Rama, so he can touch his feet: with his father gone, Rama is his father now.

original.note: Sanskrit svapna: a dream. in the epics, dreams often carry warnings of what's coming.

trapdoor: what you thought: Bharata comes home knowing what his mother did.
what it means: he's called home in the dark, and learns it all from Kaikeyi herself.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki keeps Bharata away in Kekaya through the whole crisis, which is why many readers have taken his innocence as the text's plain meaning.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 70–72 (the messengers; the journey; Kaikeyi tells Bharata)

notes: The dream's details (oil, loose hair, donkey chariot going south) are paraphrased from memory of Ayodhya 69; confirm.
The messengers' 'all is well with those you ask about' paraphrases their evasive answer; confirm.
Bharata calling Rama 'my father now' paraphrases Ayodhya 72; confirm wording.
Kekaya's direction (northwest) and the capital's name (Rajagriha/Girivraja) left general; confirm.
